paragraphs: A causal question does not always require knowing the entire network of cause and effect. Nevertheless, a common workflow first learns a complete causal graph and only then estimates the effect of an intervention. This paper combines those steps, choosing experiments around the particular causal question that needs answering.

Active Bayesian Causal Inference maintains uncertainty over both causal models and the requested answer. Model details that are not directly relevant are averaged over rather than fixed prematurely. The method repeatedly selects an informative intervention, collects its outcome, and updates its beliefs. Its implementation studies nonlinear additive Gaussian noise models with causal sufficiency, uses Gaussian processes to represent relationships, and represents graphs through continuous latent variables.

In simulations, this targeted strategy learns downstream causal quantities with fewer samples than methods concentrating on recovering the full graph. It also produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. The finding supports directing experimental effort toward the desired answer while retaining uncertainty about unresolved causal structure, within the model class studied.
neurips-2022-active-bayesian-causal-infe.tldr: ABCI chooses interventions to answer specific causal questions, improving sample efficiency in simulations while maintaining calibrated uncertainty.

paragraphs: An embodied agent may complete many tasks independently yet still struggle often enough to need assistance. Ask4Help treats requesting expert help as something an agent can learn. The aim is to improve task completion while controlling how much assistance the expert must provide.

The proposed policy augments an existing agent with the ability to request and use help. Training does not require changing the original agent’s parameters. Instead, the added policy learns a trade-off between performance and assistance, making the cost of querying an expert part of the problem. This allows help-seeking behavior to be developed around an already trained agent.

The authors evaluate object goal navigation and room rearrangement. Navigation success rises from 52% to 86% with a reported 13% help, while rearrangement success rises from 7% to 90.4% with 39% help. Human trials also support the approach’s practical effectiveness. These findings show substantial benefits from learned assistance in the evaluated tasks, with different amounts of help accompanying the two improvements.
neurips-2022-ask4help-learning-to-levera.tldr: Ask4Help learns when to request expert assistance, substantially improving embodied task success without changing the original agent’s parameters.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn successive tasks while retaining earlier abilities. Many methods protect old tasks by restricting changes to what the network has already learned. This paper examines a further possibility: carefully chosen changes during a new task could actually improve performance on earlier tasks.

The authors analyze conditions for this backward knowledge transfer using projections of gradients onto the input subspaces associated with old tasks. They then develop CUBER, which identifies positively related earlier tasks separately at different network layers. During new learning, it selectively changes the model associated with those tasks. The network has fixed capacity, and the method does not replay data from previous tasks.

On several continual learning benchmarks, CUBER achieves positive backward transfer, while the compared baselines still lose performance on earlier tasks. Better backward transfer also accompanies higher accuracy. The result supports selective adaptation as a way to improve past learning, with the theoretical analysis explaining conditions under which such updates can be beneficial.
neurips-2022-beyond-not-forgetting-conti.tldr: CUBER selectively updates knowledge from related earlier tasks, achieving positive backward transfer on several benchmarks without replaying old data.

paragraphs: Conditional independence tests ask whether two variables remain related after accounting for other variables. Such tests help causal discovery methods decide which relationships a causal graph can contain. However, commonly used tests may assume that conditional noise variance is constant, an assumption that can be unrealistic for scientific data.

This paper addresses heteroskedasticity, where that variance changes with other quantities. The authors describe it within a structural causal model and adapt the partial correlation test accordingly. Their method relies on available expert knowledge about the relationships governing heteroskedasticity. They also establish consistency results for the test, with corresponding causal discovery guarantees under additional assumptions.

Numerical causal discovery experiments show improvements over the standard partial correlation test when noise variance changes, and comparable performance when it remains constant. These results support accounting for noise structure when testing causal relationships. Expert knowledge is a substantive requirement of the approach, and the paper also examines the challenges and limits of incorporating that knowledge into causal discovery.
neurips-2022-conditional-independence-te.tldr: An adapted partial correlation test improves causal discovery with changing noise variance when expert knowledge of that variance structure is available.

paragraphs: Generating a realistic face image and controlling its three-dimensional shape are related but distinct challenges. Existing controllable image generators can change attributes such as expression or pose, yet their outputs may become inconsistent under large changes. This paper introduces explicit three-dimensional conditions to make those controls more precise.

The framework combines a NeRF-based generator with a conditional Generative Occupancy Field, or cGOF. Its central role is to make the generated face geometry conform to a mesh supplied by a 3D Morphable Model. The synthesis process also includes losses based on three-dimensional landmarks and volume warping, adding constraints intended to improve control over fine details of facial shape.

Experiments show that the method produces high-fidelity face images and offers more precise three-dimensional control than the compared state-of-the-art methods based on two-dimensional generation. The contribution is therefore both a geometry-conditioned synthesis framework and evidence that explicitly enforcing a face shape can strengthen control while retaining visual quality.
neurips-2022-controllable-3d-face-synthe.tldr: A geometry-conditioned face generator produces high-quality images with more precise 3D control than the compared 2D-based methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms are often designed through mathematical analysis, intuition, and experimentation. Automatically learning such algorithms could expand the search beyond manually chosen designs, but minimally structured black-box approaches have struggled to outperform established methods. This paper explores automatic discovery within a framework that already supplies theoretical guarantees.

That framework is Mirror Learning, which includes algorithms such as PPO while leaving some components open to design. The authors use meta-learning to discover a drift function within this space, producing Learnt Policy Optimisation, or LPO. They then analyze the learned method and use the resulting insights to formulate a new algorithm with a closed-form expression, called Discovered Policy Optimisation, or DPO.

Experiments in Brax environments report state-of-the-art performance for both LPO and DPO, together with transfer to unseen settings. The approach connects automated search with algorithm interpretation: a learned component supplies useful behavior, and analyzing it yields an explicit policy optimization method. The reported transfer supports the usefulness of the discovered designs beyond their original learning settings.
neurips-2022-discovered-policy-optimisat.tldr: Meta-learning within Mirror Learning yields LPO and inspires the closed-form DPO algorithm, both showing strong Brax performance and transfer.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates choices about a network’s design, but its use beyond well-studied vision tasks remains comparatively limited. This paper seeks a simple search strategy for diverse problems. It fixes the overall structure of a convolutional network and searches over the kernel sizes and dilations of its operations.

Those choices change the resolutions at which the network can extract features without requiring a search over its entire topology. The proposed algorithm, DASH, makes this operation search more efficient by using Fourier diagonalization of convolution to compute mixtures of candidate operations. The authors report improved asymptotic complexity and practical search speedups of up to tenfold.

Across ten tasks, including PDE solving, protein folding, and heart disease detection, DASH outperforms existing leading AutoML methods in aggregate and achieves the best-known automated performance on seven. On six tasks, search plus retraining takes less than twice the time of training a substantially less accurate CNN backbone. These results support targeted operation search as an efficient route to adapting networks across domains.
neurips-2022-efficient-architecture-sear.tldr: DASH efficiently searches convolution sizes and dilations, achieving strong automated performance across ten diverse tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization guides a search for the best experimental setting using a model of the system being studied. This paper adds occasional human input to that process. The algorithm handles the main computational search, while an expert contributes knowledge about the physical phenomenon underlying the experiment.

The expected expertise concerns how parts of the experimental system are related, rather than where the optimum lies. An expert can alter a proposed recommendation or identify promising and unpromising regions based on the observations available so far. The method uses this feedback to construct a model that better aligns with the expert’s understanding and then continues optimization using that model.

The authors provide a theoretical basis for why this collaboration may improve efficiency over optimization without expert feedback. Their empirical results report robustness, superior performance, and promising efficiency gains. The contribution is a mechanism for making partial expert understanding operational: the human need not supply the answer, but can influence how the algorithm models and searches the problem.
neurips-2022-human-ai-collaborative-baye.tldr: Occasional expert feedback shapes a Bayesian optimization model, producing promising efficiency gains without requiring experts to know the optimum.

paragraphs: An agent’s actions can be difficult to understand when success depends on a long sequence of decisions. This paper develops HEX-RL, a reinforcement learning agent designed to explain individual choices as it acts and to explain longer stretches of behavior afterward. Its setting is interactive fiction, where observations and actions are expressed in text.

HEX-RL represents the game state using an extracted symbolic knowledge graph. A hierarchical graph attention mechanism identifies facts in that internal representation that most influenced an action choice. This connects explanation generation to information used in the agent’s decision process. Text-based puzzles and quests provide tasks where both immediate actions and longer dependencies matter.

Human participants, generally unfamiliar with the environments, rate HEX-RL’s explanations significantly better than those from strong baselines. The agent also matches state-of-the-art task performance. The findings show that this architecture can combine competitive game-playing ability with explanations people judge more useful, covering both local decisions and extended trajectories rather than only isolated actions.
neurips-2022-inherently-explainable-rein.tldr: HEX-RL connects text-game decisions to knowledge-graph facts, improving human-rated explanations while matching state-of-the-art task performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a surface from a point cloud requires turning scattered samples into coherent geometry. Signed distance approaches are limited to closed surfaces in the methods discussed here. Unsigned distance functions can also represent open surfaces, but learning a smooth field near the surface is difficult when the observations are discrete points.

This paper learns an unsigned distance function directly from raw point clouds. It trains a network to move three-dimensional query points toward an estimated surface while enforcing consistency in the surrounding field. The surface estimate improves progressively, and the method dynamically searches for the targets toward which queries should move. This lets the relationship between queries and the estimated geometry evolve during learning.

The authors also introduce a polygonization algorithm that extracts a surface directly from the learned function’s gradient field. Experiments using synthetic data and real scans report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. Together, the learning and extraction procedures address both constructing a consistent distance representation and converting it into a reconstructed surface.
neurips-2022-learning-consistency-aware-.tldr: Progressive learning with field consistency reconstructs surfaces from raw point clouds through an unsigned distance representation.

paragraphs: A row in a table can contain useful predictive information on its own, but related rows may provide additional context. This paper studies how to use that context to directly improve the representation of a target row. Its proposed model, PET, combines retrieval of relevant instances with information propagation between them.

PET first constructs a hypergraph from the retrieved instances to represent patterns across both rows and columns. A specially designed message-passing step then enhances the target representation. It combines features with labels during propagation and uses locality-aware multiplicative interactions among multiple features. The resulting representation therefore incorporates information from the neighborhood alongside relationships among the features themselves.

Experiments on two tabular prediction tasks show PET outperforming the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies and visualizations also support the usefulness of its components and its ability to enhance representations. The contribution is a concrete method for integrating related examples into prediction, with the reported results indicating benefits from jointly modeling cross-row context and richer feature interactions.
neurips-2022-learning-enhanced-represent.tldr: PET improves tabular representations by propagating features and labels through a hypergraph of related rows.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image generation builds an image representation through a sequence of predictions. This paper organizes that representation into local hierarchies, separating coarse structure from fine details. The aim is to retain image fidelity while reducing the computation needed to generate the underlying discrete codes.

The first stage, HQ-VAE, represents an image as a pyramid of codes. In the two-level example, upper codes carry broad structure, while lower codes use a residual pathway to capture missing detail. Choices of resizing operations help the upper codes retain information. The second stage, HQ-Transformer, processes local pyramids containing one upper code and its associated lower codes.

Generation samples the lower codes in parallel using a conditional independence assumption motivated by their role as local-detail representations. This assumption enables a less costly generation procedure. On class-conditioned and text-conditioned benchmarks, the method produces images with fidelity competitive with earlier autoregressive models while using lighter computational budgets. The results connect the organization of the learned codes with the efficiency of subsequent generation.
neurips-2022-locally-hierarchical-auto-r.tldr: Hierarchical image codes enable parallel generation of local details, delivering competitive image fidelity with lighter computational budgets.

paragraphs: LogiGAN aims to strengthen a language model’s logical reasoning through unsupervised pre-training. It uses heuristics to find reasoning-related statements in a large text collection, masks selected statements, and trains models to predict them. This creates a learning task centered on logical content found automatically in existing text.

The framework pairs a Generator with a Verifier in an adversarial architecture inspired by reflective learning. To handle the difficulty of differentiating through generated text sequences, the Generator also serves as a sentence-level likelihood scorer and learns to bring its scores into agreement with the Verifier. The resulting sequential GAN approach is designed to remain computationally feasible for large-scale pre-training with arbitrary target lengths.

Both base-sized and large models improve across twelve datasets requiring general reasoning. Component ablations suggest that linguistic ability and logical ability are relatively distinct, and that the reflective-learning analogy may extend to machine learning. These findings support the usefulness of the training framework while keeping the broader interpretation about reflective thinking tentative.
neurips-2022-logigan-learning-logical-re.tldr: LogiGAN uses adversarial Generator–Verifier pre-training on automatically identified logical statements to improve language-model reasoning.

paragraphs: Neural network training is generally nonconvex, yet gradient descent can still find globally optimal solutions in some overparameterized settings. This paper studies that phenomenon for residual networks whose blocks depend linearly on their parameters while remaining nonlinear functions. The construction connects analyses of networks with finite and infinite size.

In the infinite-depth and infinite-width limit, the residual blocks belong to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The authors prove a local Polyak–Lojasiewicz inequality, which relates optimization error to gradient information. Their analysis establishes that every critical point is a global minimizer and gives a local convergence result for gradient descent. It covers parametric and nonparametric cases under an expressivity condition on the residual blocks.

The paper also translates the analysis into a quantified construction for finite models. Starting from a universal kernel space, Random Fourier Features produce a finite-dimensional parameterization satisfying the expressivity condition with high probability. This links the theoretical condition to a practical model-building recipe, while preserving the local scope of the gradient-descent convergence result.
neurips-2022-on-global-convergence-of-re.tldr: For a structured class of ResNets, the paper connects convergence theory to finite parameterizations satisfying an expressivity condition with high probability.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model can aim to increase rewards for preferred outputs or to match an explicitly specified output distribution. This paper examines the theoretical relationship between those two approaches. The distinction matters because a desired distribution can express requirements about how frequently different kinds of text should appear.

The authors show that some methods usually described as reward maximization, including KL-control, can also be interpreted as distribution matching. They also observe that distribution matching can experience training problems familiar from reinforcement learning, such as high gradient variance. Using the connection between the approaches, they introduce the concept of a baseline into distribution-matching methods to improve training.

Experiments cover controllable generation tasks involving topic, sentiment, and gender distributions. Adding a baseline produces better constraint satisfaction, training stability, and sample efficiency in the reported evaluations. The contribution is both a conceptual bridge between fine-tuning paradigms and a practical training improvement derived from it, showing how techniques developed for one objective can benefit another.
neurips-2022-on-reinforcement-learning-a.tldr: Connecting reward maximization with distribution matching yields a baseline technique that improves controlled language generation training.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis tries to recover independent hidden sources from observations that mix them nonlinearly. A central difficulty is identifiability: whether the observations determine those sources, apart from accepted ambiguities. Recent approaches use auxiliary information such as labels or time indices, but that route does not address models with unconditional source priors.

This paper instead imposes assumptions on the mixing process, including structural sparsity. Under specific forms of these constraints, the authors prove that the latent sources can be identified up to reordering and a separate transformation of each source. The result provides nontrivial identifiability without requiring auxiliary variables, while explicitly retaining those remaining ambiguities.

The authors also provide estimation methods and test their theoretical findings experimentally. Results on image data suggest that the proposed conditions may occur in practical data-generating processes. The contribution is an alternative set of sufficient structural conditions for source recovery, with experimental evidence supporting their possible relevance beyond purely theoretical constructions.
neurips-2022-on-the-identifiability-of-n.tldr: Specific structural constraints on nonlinear mixing make independent sources identifiable without auxiliary variables, up to stated ambiguities.

paragraphs: Neural networks can fit their training data closely while performing poorly on future examples. Regularization aims to control this tendency, but different regularizers are often motivated by different principles. This paper introduces Model Gradient Similarity, or MGS, as a framework for examining their behavior through a shared measure.

MGS serves three connected purposes. It provides a metric of regularization that can be monitored during training, offers an interpretation of how explicit regularizers work, and forms the basis of a new regularization method. The authors describe an underlying common mechanism in which regularizers increase MGS. This connects methods with different starting motivations through their effect on model gradient similarity.

The proposed MGS-based regularization scheme is reported to perform especially well with noisy labels or limited training samples. Those findings make the framework relevant both for understanding training and for changing it. Its contribution is therefore broader than a new penalty alone: it links a monitoring quantity, an explanation of regularization behavior, and a method built from that explanation.
neurips-2022-on-the-interpretability-of-.tldr: Model Gradient Similarity provides a shared interpretation of regularization and motivates a method effective with noisy labels or limited data.

paragraphs: Learning dynamics in a game can keep cycling instead of settling at a Nash equilibrium. This paper shows that such behavior can still lead to a strong equilibrium guarantee for average play. It studies general-sum two-player games in which both players use optimistic mirror descent with smooth regularization.

For sufficiently small approximation tolerance, an appropriately small learning rate, and enough repetitions, the authors establish two possible outcomes. Either the dynamics reach an approximate Nash equilibrium, or the average joint distribution of play becomes a strong coarse correlated equilibrium. In the latter case, switching unilaterally to a fixed alternative action decreases a player’s expected utility by a quantitatively bounded amount.

If the iterates remain bounded away from Nash equilibria, the analysis also gives convergence to an exact coarse correlated equilibrium after a constant number of iterations. The proof shows that both players’ cumulative regret becomes negative and decreases linearly over time. Thus, continued cycling can accompany efficient equilibrium learning, with the guarantee applying to accumulated play rather than requiring the current strategies to settle.
neurips-2022-optimistic-mirror-descent-e.tldr: Under stated conditions, optimistic mirror descent reaches approximate Nash equilibrium or produces average play with a strong coarse correlated equilibrium guarantee.

paragraphs: Stereo matching finds correspondences between two views of a scene. This paper asks whether strong neural stereo systems actually learn reliable matching. It develops white-box attacks constrained to remain consistent across the stereo pair and photometrically consistent. Despite these restrictions, the attacks cause severe performance drops, suggesting weaknesses in the matching behavior learned by the tested networks.

The proposed response combines binary-pattern-based nonparametric matching cost volumes with neural contextualization and learned cost aggregation. The design is trainable end to end and does not require specific aggregation inductive biases. It addresses both adversarial vulnerability and the photometric gap between simulated training images and real images.

Experiments on SceneFlow, KITTI2015, and Middlebury show significantly improved adversarial robustness while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The approach also improves simulation-to-real generalization. These findings support revisiting the construction of matching costs as part of neural stereo design, with benefits for both attack resistance and transfer across image domains.
neurips-2022-revisiting-non-parametric-m.tldr: Combining nonparametric matching costs with neural aggregation improves stereo robustness and simulation-to-real generalization while retaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Adversarial changes need not be small numerical perturbations. In program analysis and security, an attacker may transform an input through a sequence of logically related versions. This paper formalizes such relational adversaries using all inputs reachable through zero or more applications of a specified logical relation.

The authors analyze conditions for robustness and how different patterns in the relation affect the trade-off between robustness and accuracy. Their resulting framework, normalize-and-predict, uses input normalization to obtain provable robustness. It addresses difficulties encountered by adversarial training in this setting and can also be combined with adversarial training to draw on both approaches.

The framework is evaluated on source code authorship attribution and malware detection. In both tasks, it significantly improves robustness against relational adversaries and outperforms adversarial training by a wide margin. The work therefore expands the kind of transformations a robustness framework can address, while connecting its defense mechanism to a theoretical analysis of the permitted relationships between inputs.
neurips-2022-robust-learning-against-rel.tldr: Normalize-and-predict provides provable robustness against relational transformations and improves defenses in code attribution and malware detection.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a sparse signal is present can become substantially harder when some observations are arbitrarily corrupted. This paper establishes sample requirements for robust signal testing in two high-dimensional models. The question is whether a signal is zero or has magnitude above a specified threshold, rather than how accurately to reconstruct every coordinate.

The first model uses independent Gaussian observations with identity covariance and an unknown mean having at most s nonzero coordinates. The authors prove a sample lower bound proportional to s log(ed/s), where d is the dimension, and show it is tight up to logarithmic factors. They also extend the results to sparsity constraints expressed using q-norms for q between zero and two.

The second model is sparse linear regression with Gaussian covariates and an arbitrarily corrupted fraction of the data. Its sample lower bound scales as the minimum of s log d and 1/γ⁴, where γ is the signal threshold. These lower bounds establish that robustness increases the intrinsic data requirements of testing in the studied settings.
neurips-2022-robust-testing-in-high-dime.tldr: Sample lower bounds show that arbitrary data corruption substantially increases the difficulty of detecting sparse high-dimensional signals.

paragraphs: Learning from unlabeled scene images requires handling several meaningful objects or regions within one picture. Existing approaches often introduce manually designed assumptions about objects or specialized training tasks. SlotCon instead learns semantic groups and visual representations together, allowing the grouping structure to emerge from the data.

The method assigns pixels to learnable prototypes. Attention-based pooling adapts those prototypes to the features in each image, forming image-dependent slots. A contrastive objective then trains representations using these slots. The two processes reinforce one another: more discriminative features help group semantically related pixels, and the groups provide units for learning useful features.

Experiments show that SlotCon decomposes complex scenes into semantic groups and improves downstream object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. The contribution is a coupled learning framework that develops group-level representations from unlabeled scenes without relying on the handcrafted objectness priors described in earlier work. Its reported downstream benefits indicate that the learned grouping supports tasks requiring more localized understanding than a single whole-image representation.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-visual-repr.tldr: SlotCon jointly learns semantic pixel groups and contrastive representations from unlabeled scenes, improving detection and segmentation tasks.

paragraphs: Learned feature vectors are often compared using their angles, even though ordinary neural network computations can encode information in both direction and magnitude. Using only angular similarity may then discard useful information. This paper introduces a spherization layer designed to place representation information into angular relationships during learning.

The layer maps pre-activation values into a specified angular range, converts the resulting angular coordinates into Cartesian coordinates with one additional dimension, and learns decision boundaries using bias-free hyperplanes through the origin. This construction keeps representation learning on a hyperspherical surface. The authors establish information preservation for the construction, distinguishing it from projection-based approaches that can lose information.

The layer can replace an existing layer in a network. Evaluations examine functional correctness on a toy task, information retention in image classification, and effectiveness in word analogy and few-shot learning. These tests address different aspects of the proposal: whether the mapping behaves as intended, whether representations retain useful content, and whether angular representations support downstream use.
neurips-2022-spherization-layer-represen.tldr: The spherization layer learns information-preserving representations on a hypersphere so that information is expressed through angles.

paragraphs: Vision transformers process images as sequences of patches. This paper finds that their predictions can remain surprisingly insensitive to patch transformations that destroy recognizable image meaning. The observation points to reliance on features that survive those changes even though people would not generally use them to identify the image’s semantic class.

Further experiments show that these features can support high accuracy on the training distribution yet fail under distribution shifts. The authors use the transformed images as negative augmentations and introduce training losses that discourage dependence on the surviving non-robust features. This complements conventional augmentation, which usually preserves meaning and encourages predictions to stay consistent.

Across more than twenty experimental settings on ImageNet-based robustness benchmarks, patch-based negative augmentation consistently improves vision transformer robustness. It also complements traditional positive augmentation and batch-based negative examples in contrastive learning. The results show how deliberately damaging semantic content can provide a useful training signal about which features a model should rely on less.
neurips-2022-understanding-and-improving.tldr: Patch transformations expose non-robust vision-transformer features and provide negative training examples that improve robustness.

paragraphs: Cross-entropy is the dominant loss for neural network classification, but empirical work has renewed interest in square loss. This paper develops a theoretical account of square loss for overparameterized classifiers in the neural tangent kernel regime. It studies prediction error, robustness, and calibration, meaning how well reported confidence corresponds to correctness.

The analysis separates cases in which classes are separable from those in which they are not. In the general nonseparable setting, it establishes fast convergence rates for misclassification and calibration error. With separable classes, misclassification improves at an exponential rate. The authors also prove that the resulting margin stays bounded away from zero, yielding a theoretical robustness guarantee.

Experiments on practical networks use both synthetic low-dimensional data and real images. Compared with cross-entropy, square loss achieves comparable generalization error and noticeable advantages in robustness and calibration. These observations support practical usefulness beyond the theoretical setting, while the authors’ expectation that their findings extend beyond the neural tangent kernel regime remains broader than the established analysis.
neurips-2022-understanding-square-loss-i.tldr: Square loss receives classification guarantees in the neural tangent kernel regime and shows practical robustness and calibration advantages over cross-entropy.
